title: Acids, Bases and Salts
description: Grade 7 Chemistry: Acids, Bases and Salts — concept notes, solved examples, key-point recaps, per-topic quizzes and free online tests.

topics.title: Acids — Properties and Common Acids
topics.concept:
The substances we meet in daily life can often be sorted by their chemical nature into acids, bases, and salts. An acid is a substance that tastes sour and turns blue litmus paper red. The word "acid" comes from a Latin word meaning sour. Many familiar foods owe their sour taste to acids: lemons and oranges contain citric acid, vinegar contains acetic acid, curd and sour milk contain lactic acid, and tamarind contains tartaric acid. These acids found in food and living things are called organic acids and are generally weak and safe in small amounts.

Some acids are made and used in laboratories and industry. These are called mineral acids and include hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄), and nitric acid (HNO₃). Mineral acids are usually strong and can be very corrosive, meaning they can eat away skin, cloth, and metals. They must always be handled with great care, and strong acids should never be tasted or touched. Interestingly, our own stomach produces dilute hydrochloric acid, which helps in the digestion of food.

Acids share a set of common properties. They taste sour (though we never taste laboratory acids), they turn blue litmus red, and many of them react with metals to release hydrogen gas. They also react with bases in a special reaction called neutralisation, which we will study later. Because strong acids are corrosive, they are stored carefully and diluted by always adding acid slowly to water (never water to acid), as mixing the wrong way can splash dangerously.

Acids are extremely useful. Sulphuric acid is so important to industry that it is sometimes called the "king of chemicals"; it is used in fertilisers, batteries, and many manufacturing processes. Acids are also used in food preservation, in cleaning, and in our own bodies for digestion.

examples.problem: Example 1: A liquid tastes sour and turns blue litmus paper red. What is its chemical nature?
examples.solution:
Use the two key tests for an acid.

  • A sour taste is a property of acids.
  • Turning blue litmus red is the standard test for an acid.
  • Answer: The liquid is acidic in nature (it is an acid).
examples.answer: The liquid is acidic in nature (it is an acid).

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the acid present in (a) lemon, (b) vinegar, and (c) curd.
examples.solution:
Each food contains a particular organic acid.

  • Lemon contains citric acid; vinegar contains acetic acid.
  • Curd (sour milk) contains lactic acid.
  • Answer: (a) citric acid, (b) acetic acid, (c) lactic acid.
examples.answer: (a) citric acid, (b) acetic acid, (c) lactic acid.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why should a strong acid like sulphuric acid always be diluted by adding the acid to water, and not water to the acid?
examples.solution:
Diluting an acid releases a lot of heat.

  • Adding acid slowly to water lets the heat spread safely through the larger amount of water.
  • Adding water to concentrated acid produces heat too quickly and can make the acid splash out dangerously.
  • Answer: Acid is added to water so the heat released is absorbed safely, preventing dangerous splashing.
examples.answer: Acid is added to water so the heat released is absorbed safely, preventing dangerous splashing.

recap:
• An acid tastes sour and turns blue litmus paper red.
  • Organic acids occur in foods: citric acid (lemon), acetic acid (vinegar), lactic acid (curd), tartaric acid (tamarind).
  • Mineral acids made in laboratories include hydrochloric (HCl), sulphuric (H₂SO₄), and nitric (HNO₃) acid; they are strong and corrosive.
  • Many acids react with metals to release hydrogen gas; the stomach uses dilute HCl for digestion.
  • A strong acid must always be diluted by adding acid slowly to water, never water to acid.

quiz.explanation: Acids characteristically taste sour, like lemon and vinegar.

quiz.q: An acid turns litmus paper which colour?
quiz.explanation: Acids turn blue litmus paper red, the standard test for an acid.

quiz.q: The acid present in vinegar is:
quiz.explanation: Vinegar contains acetic acid, an organic acid.

quiz.q: Which of these is a strong mineral acid?
quiz.explanation: Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) is a strong, corrosive mineral acid.

quiz.q: The acid produced in the human stomach to help digestion is:
quiz.explanation: The stomach secretes dilute hydrochloric acid to aid digestion.

topics.title: Bases — Properties and Common Bases
topics.concept:
A base is a substance that is the chemical opposite of an acid. Bases generally taste bitter and feel soapy or slippery to the touch, and they turn red litmus paper blue. Many household substances are basic: baking soda, soap and detergents, lime water, toothpaste, and window-cleaning liquids are all bases. The bitterness of these substances and the slippery feel of soap are typical signs of a base.

A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali. All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis (some bases do not dissolve in water). Common examples of bases and alkalis include sodium hydroxide (NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH), calcium hydroxide [Ca(OH)₂] (slaked lime, which forms lime water), and magnesium hydroxide [Mg(OH)₂] (the main ingredient in many antacids, "milk of magnesia"). Strong bases such as sodium hydroxide are highly corrosive, just like strong acids, and must be handled carefully.

Bases share common properties that mirror those of acids. They taste bitter (laboratory bases are never tasted), feel soapy, and turn red litmus blue. They also react with acids in a neutralisation reaction to form a salt and water, cancelling out each other's effects. Because strong bases are corrosive, they too require careful handling and proper storage.

Bases are very useful in everyday life and industry. Sodium hydroxide is used in making soap, paper, and textiles; calcium hydroxide (lime) is used in whitewashing walls and in agriculture to reduce soil acidity; magnesium hydroxide and other mild bases are used as antacids to relieve acidity in the stomach. Understanding bases alongside acids helps us see how the two opposites are used together in cooking, cleaning, medicine, and farming.

examples.problem: Example 1: A substance feels soapy, tastes bitter, and turns red litmus paper blue. What is its chemical nature?
examples.solution:
Apply the tests for a base.

  • A bitter taste and soapy feel are properties of bases.
  • Turning red litmus blue is the standard test for a base.
  • Answer: The substance is basic in nature (it is a base).
examples.answer: The substance is basic in nature (it is a base).

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the difference between a base and an alkali?
examples.solution:
Compare their relationship to water.

  • A base is any substance that turns red litmus blue and neutralises acids.
  • An alkali is a base that dissolves in water; all alkalis are bases, but not all bases dissolve.
  • Answer: A base is the general class; an alkali is specifically a base that dissolves in water.
examples.answer: A base is the general class; an alkali is specifically a base that dissolves in water.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is magnesium hydroxide used in antacid medicines?
examples.solution:
Antacids treat excess stomach acid.

  • The stomach sometimes produces too much hydrochloric acid, causing acidity.
  • Magnesium hydroxide is a mild base that neutralises this excess acid.
  • Answer: Magnesium hydroxide is used in antacids because, being a mild base, it neutralises the excess acid in the stomach.
examples.answer: Magnesium hydroxide is used in antacids because, being a mild base, it neutralises the excess acid in the stomach.

recap:
• A base tastes bitter, feels soapy, and turns red litmus paper blue.
  • An alkali is a base that dissolves in water; all alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis.
  • Common bases include sodium hydroxide (NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH), calcium hydroxide [Ca(OH)₂], and magnesium hydroxide [Mg(OH)₂].
  • Bases react with acids in neutralisation to form salt and water; strong bases like NaOH are corrosive.
  • Bases are used in soap, paper, whitewashing, reducing soil acidity, and as antacids.

quiz.explanation: Bases taste bitter and feel soapy, opposite to the sour taste of acids.

quiz.q: A base turns litmus paper which colour?
quiz.explanation: Bases turn red litmus paper blue, the standard test for a base.

quiz.q: A base that dissolves in water is called a/an:
quiz.explanation: A base that dissolves in water is specifically called an alkali.

quiz.q: Which substance is used in many antacids to relieve stomach acidity?
quiz.explanation: Magnesium hydroxide, a mild base, neutralises excess stomach acid.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a strong, corrosive base?
quiz.explanation: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is a strong, corrosive base.

topics.title: Indicators
topics.concept:
We cannot, and must not, find out whether a substance is acidic or basic by tasting or touching it, especially in the laboratory. Instead, scientists use special substances called indicators. An indicator is a substance that changes its colour to tell us whether a given substance is an acid or a base. The colour change acts as a clear, safe signal of the chemical nature of the substance.

The most common indicator is litmus, a natural dye extracted from a plant-like organism called lichen. Litmus is available as a solution and as litmus paper in two colours, blue and red. Acids turn blue litmus red, and bases turn red litmus blue. A neutral substance, such as pure water, does not change the colour of either type of litmus paper. Litmus is the simplest indicator for telling acids and bases apart.

There are several other useful indicators. Phenolphthalein is a synthetic indicator that stays colourless in acids and turns pink in bases. Methyl orange turns red in acids and yellow in bases. There are also many natural indicators that we can prepare at home: turmeric stays yellow in acids but turns red (or reddish-brown) in bases — which is why a turmeric stain on cloth turns red when soap is rubbed on it; red cabbage extract changes through a range of colours; and the petals of flowers such as the China rose (hibiscus) can also be used as indicators.

Indicators are extremely valuable in science and daily life. They allow us to test substances safely and quickly, to follow the progress of a neutralisation reaction, to check the acidity of soil for farming, and to monitor the quality of water. By simply watching a colour change, we learn the chemical nature of a substance without any risk of tasting or touching it.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is an indicator, and why is it useful?
examples.solution:
Consider how we safely test substances.

  • An indicator is a substance that changes colour to show whether a substance is an acid or a base.
  • It lets us test substances safely without tasting or touching them.
  • Answer: An indicator is a colour-changing substance that safely tells us whether something is an acid or a base.
examples.answer: An indicator is a colour-changing substance that safely tells us whether something is an acid or a base.

examples.problem: Example 2: A few drops of phenolphthalein are added to a solution and it turns pink. What is the nature of the solution?
examples.solution:
Recall the colours of phenolphthalein.

  • Phenolphthalein is colourless in acids and turns pink in bases.
  • The solution turned pink.
  • Answer: The solution is basic (a base), because phenolphthalein turns pink only in bases.
examples.answer: The solution is basic (a base), because phenolphthalein turns pink only in bases.

examples.problem: Example 3: A yellow turmeric stain on a white cloth turns red when soap is rubbed on it. Explain why.
examples.solution:
Turmeric acts as a natural indicator.

  • Turmeric is yellow in acidic or neutral conditions but turns red in a base.
  • Soap is basic, so rubbing it on the turmeric stain provides a base.
  • Answer: Soap is a base, and turmeric turns red in a base, so the stain changes from yellow to red.
examples.answer: Soap is a base, and turmeric turns red in a base, so the stain changes from yellow to red.

recap:
• An indicator is a substance that changes colour to show whether a substance is an acid or a base.
  • Litmus (from lichen) is the commonest indicator: acids turn blue litmus red and bases turn red litmus blue.
  • Phenolphthalein is colourless in acids and pink in bases; methyl orange is red in acids and yellow in bases.
  • Natural indicators include turmeric (yellow in acid, red in base), red cabbage extract, and China rose petals.
  • Indicators allow safe, quick testing of substances without tasting or touching them.

quiz.q: A substance that changes colour to show if something is an acid or base is a/an:
quiz.explanation: An indicator signals the acidic or basic nature of a substance by changing colour.

quiz.q: Litmus is a natural dye obtained from:
quiz.explanation: Litmus is extracted from lichens.

quiz.q: Phenolphthalein turns which colour in a basic solution?
quiz.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acids and turns pink in bases.

quiz.q: Turmeric, a natural indicator, turns red in the presence of a:
quiz.explanation: Turmeric is yellow in acid/neutral and turns red in a base.

quiz.q: Methyl orange turns red in the presence of a/an:
quiz.explanation: Methyl orange is red in acids and yellow in bases.

topics.title: The pH Scale
topics.concept:
Indicators like litmus can tell us whether a substance is acidic or basic, but they do not tell us how strong the acid or base is. To measure the strength of acidity or basicity, scientists use the pH scale. The pH scale is a set of numbers running from 0 to 14 that tells us how acidic or basic a solution is. The letters "pH" stand for the "power of hydrogen", as the value depends on the amount of hydrogen present in the solution.

On the pH scale, a value of exactly 7 means the solution is neutral — neither acidic nor basic — like pure water. A value less than 7 means the solution is acidic: the lower the number, the stronger the acid, so a substance of pH 1 or 2 (such as stomach acid or lemon juice) is strongly acidic. A value greater than 7 means the solution is basic (alkaline): the higher the number, the stronger the base, so a substance of pH 13 or 14 (such as sodium hydroxide solution) is strongly basic.

The pH of a solution can be found quickly using universal indicator, which is a mixture of several indicators that shows a whole range of colours for different pH values — typically red for strong acids, through orange, yellow, and green for neutral, to blue and violet for strong bases. By matching the colour to a chart, we can read off the approximate pH. More precise measurements are made with a digital instrument called a pH meter.

Knowing pH is important in many areas of life. Our blood must stay very close to pH 7.4, and even small changes can be harmful. Soil pH affects how well crops grow, so farmers test and adjust it. The pH of rainwater, rivers, and aquariums is monitored to protect living things, and pH balance matters in foods, medicines, cosmetics, and toothpastes. The pH scale therefore turns the idea of "acidic" or "basic" into a precise, useful number.

examples.problem: Example 1: A solution has a pH of 3. Is it acidic, basic, or neutral, and is it strong or weak?
examples.solution:
Compare the value with 7.

  • A pH less than 7 means the solution is acidic.
  • A pH of 3 is well below 7, so it is a fairly strong acid.
  • Answer: The solution is acidic and fairly strong, since its pH (3) is well below 7.
examples.answer: The solution is acidic and fairly strong, since its pH (3) is well below 7.

examples.problem: Example 2: What does a pH value of exactly 7 indicate?
examples.solution:
Recall the meaning of 7 on the scale.

  • A pH of 7 is the middle of the scale.
  • It means the solution is neither acidic nor basic.
  • Answer: A pH of 7 indicates a neutral solution, such as pure water.
examples.answer: A pH of 7 indicates a neutral solution, such as pure water.

examples.problem: Example 3: Two solutions have pH values of 1 and 5. Which one is the stronger acid?
examples.solution:
Compare the two values below 7.

  • Both are acidic, as both are below 7.
  • The lower the pH, the stronger the acid, and 1 is lower than 5.
  • Answer: The solution with pH 1 is the stronger acid.
examples.answer: The solution with pH 1 is the stronger acid.

recap:
• The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and measures how acidic or basic a solution is ("pH" = power of hydrogen).
  • A pH of exactly 7 is neutral (e.g. pure water); below 7 is acidic; above 7 is basic (alkaline).
  • The lower the pH below 7, the stronger the acid; the higher the pH above 7, the stronger the base.
  • Universal indicator shows a range of colours for different pH values; a pH meter gives precise readings.
  • pH matters in blood (≈7.4), soil for crops, water bodies, foods, medicines, and cosmetics.

quiz.q: The pH scale runs over the range of values from:
quiz.explanation: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14, measuring acidity and basicity.

quiz.q: A solution with a pH of exactly 7 is:
quiz.explanation: A pH of 7 is neutral, like pure water.

quiz.q: A solution with a pH less than 7 is:
quiz.explanation: A pH below 7 means the solution is acidic.

quiz.q: As the pH value rises above 7, the solution becomes increasingly:
quiz.explanation: Values above 7 are basic, and the higher the value, the stronger the base.

quiz.q: Which solution is the strongest acid?
quiz.explanation: The lower the pH below 7, the stronger the acid; pH 2 is the strongest here.

topics.title: Neutralisation, Salts and Acid Rain
topics.concept:
When an acid and a base are mixed together in the right amounts, they cancel out each other's properties. This reaction between an acid and a base is called neutralisation. In a neutralisation reaction, the acid and base react to form a salt and water, and a large amount of heat is usually released. The general word equation is: acid + base → salt + water. For example, hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide to give common salt (sodium chloride) and water.

A salt is the compound formed when the acid and base neutralise each other. Salts are usually neutral, though some can be slightly acidic or basic. The most familiar salt is sodium chloride (NaCl), common table salt, formed from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide. Other useful salts include sodium sulphate (Na₂SO₄) and many salts used in fertilisers, medicines, and food. Salts are an important class of chemical compounds with countless everyday uses.

Neutralisation is at work in many everyday situations. When we suffer from acidity in the stomach (too much acid), we take an antacid, which is a mild base that neutralises the excess acid and relieves the pain. A bee or ant sting injects an acid that causes pain; rubbing a mild base such as baking soda on the sting neutralises it. Soil that is too acidic is treated with lime (a base) to neutralise it, and soil that is too basic is treated with compost or other acidic matter. Even toothpaste, which is basic, neutralises the acids formed by bacteria in the mouth and protects the teeth.

A harmful effect related to acids in the environment is acid rain. When fuels are burnt, gases such as sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides are released into the air. These gases dissolve in rainwater to form acids, making the rain acidic — this is acid rain. Acid rain damages buildings and monuments (especially marble ones such as the Taj Mahal, in a process sometimes called "marble cancer"), harms plants and forests, and makes the water of rivers and lakes acidic, threatening fish and other aquatic life. Reducing the burning of polluting fuels helps prevent acid rain.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is neutralisation, and what are its products?
examples.solution:
Consider what happens when an acid meets a base.

  • An acid and a base react together and cancel out each other's properties.
  • This reaction produces a salt and water (and releases heat).
  • Answer: Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water.
examples.answer: Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water.

examples.problem: Example 2: A person suffering from acidity in the stomach is given an antacid. Explain how it helps.
examples.solution:
Acidity is caused by excess acid.

  • The stomach has produced too much hydrochloric acid, causing discomfort.
  • The antacid is a mild base that neutralises this excess acid.
  • Answer: The antacid, being a base, neutralises the excess stomach acid, relieving the acidity.
examples.answer: The antacid, being a base, neutralises the excess stomach acid, relieving the acidity.

examples.problem: Example 3: How does acid rain damage marble monuments such as the Taj Mahal?
examples.solution:
Marble reacts with acid.

  • Acid rain contains acids formed from polluting gases dissolved in rainwater.
  • These acids react with and slowly eat away the marble (calcium carbonate) of the monument.
  • Answer: The acids in acid rain react with and corrode the marble, slowly damaging monuments like the Taj Mahal.
examples.answer: The acids in acid rain react with and corrode the marble, slowly damaging monuments like the Taj Mahal.

recap:
• Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base, producing a salt and water and releasing heat: acid + base → salt + water.
  • A salt is the compound formed in neutralisation; the most common is sodium chloride (NaCl), common table salt.
  • Everyday neutralisation includes antacids for stomach acidity, baking soda on insect stings, and lime to treat acidic soil.
  • Acid rain forms when polluting gases (like sulphur and nitrogen oxides) dissolve in rainwater, making it acidic.
  • Acid rain damages buildings and monuments, harms plants, and makes water bodies acidic, threatening aquatic life.
